statement: Coordination below national level is largely sustained by people who already hold another full-time role. Dedicated subnational posts are rare, are among the first affected when budgets tighten, and functions continue to be added — wider assessment coverage, growing pooled fund portfolios, disaggregation previously produced elsewhere — to structures whose staffing has not grown. Where the post is vacant or held at a fraction of time, attendance at meetings continues but the work that carries deadlines does not.

Coordinator and information management posts are reduced before programme staff when budgets fall, including subnational posts funded through lead agency partnership agreements, which are not renewed. Because coordination is funded agency by agency rather than as a shared function, capacity varies between sectors in the same operation according to what each lead agency can still cover.

Information management capacity is reduced earlier and further than other coordination capacity: recruitment cancelled, posts frozen, downgraded to volunteer arrangements, or filled below the level the role requires. The resulting constraint is analytical rather than one of data availability — partner reporting continues to arrive while dashboards, contact lists and reconciliation work fall behind. The subnational profile is also hard to fill, because the work is embedded and continuous rather than a short deployment, and where collection relies on volunteers the tools have to be kept simple enough for them.

Incoming coordinators frequently arrive without a handover and reconstruct the picture from shared drives, losing time to work already done. Where the link to another structure runs through an individual rather than an institutional arrangement, it ends when that person leaves.

Government leadership rests on individual counterparts. A ministry reshuffle or an election moves the trained official, and the case for coordination has to be made again from the beginning with people who do not yet see its value. Capacity behaves as a flow that rotation continuously drains rather than a stock that training builds once, which is why institutional anchoring matters more than training individuals.

The structures expected to receive coordination are rarely resourced for it. Co-leading ministries commonly have one trained focal point, no information management function and no institutional home for humanitarian coordination, and a single official may carry a workload that previously sat with several. National NGOs and public utilities identified as successors have been found unable to carry what an emergency places on them, and at least one transition plan is being reopened for that reason. Roles and mandates are often not set out clearly to the actors expected to take them on. Long-standing sector investment has not on its own produced absorptive capacity where governance arrangements did not change alongside it.

Coordination capacity placed inside government does not automatically carry authority. A government technical cell can be established and still lack access to intersectoral fora, with partners hesitant to engage it directly and its attention defaulting to government's own activities. Embedded staff are difficult to hold to coordination terms of reference inside a government hierarchy, and jointly designed posts have reached final shortlists without the ministry taking them up.

Area-based structures are not consistently required or resourced to hold sector technical capacity. Terms of reference set no technical requirement for focal points; several pilots depended on external facilitation rather than local capacity; and where sector coordination has been subordinated to area structures, the functions that depend on technical staffing — operational gap analysis in particular — have lost their platform, which shows most during sudden emergencies. Adding further functions such as preparedness to structures already short of core capacity is unrealistic. Coordinators across several contexts are asking what needs to be in place before functions move, and the question does not yet have a settled answer.

Capacity development runs on funding envelopes shorter and less predictable than the engagement it requires. Organisations tasked with building local capacity work on short and volatile grants, and training has been reduced in scope or moved online for cost reasons.

Planned coordination work is repeatedly displaced by emergency and process demands. Commitments carried in the workplan for years remain unstarted because each year's emergencies force reprioritisation; external process changes arriving at short notice absorb meeting time; and capacity building programmes have been scheduled into planning peaks before being rephased.

A new emergency interrupts transition. Where a sudden escalation triggers a flash appeal, coordination ownership has returned to the lead agency and the successor actors built up during the calmer period are set aside at the moment they would learn most by doing. Cyclical crises can overtake a transition plan before it takes hold. Platforms cycle rather than end: several have moved between government leadership, national society leadership, deactivation and reactivation.

Partner technical capacity is thin in specific areas. Weak local implementation capacity translates directly into uneven service delivery, and specialised areas such as faecal sludge management in displacement sites have few partners with relevant experience.

A national co-coordinator anchored in an institution rather than in a single post carries continuity through and after the departure of international staff. Working in the national language, recruited with an overlap period before the outgoing coordinator leaves, and paired with a national information management position, this arrangement has held processes together for a year or more. Where sectors nationalised both posts they continued to function; retaining one while removing the other has not worked in practice.

Embedding coordination capacity in government works where government asks for it and the investment is sustained. Posts requested at senior government level and recruited through third-party contracting, joint training with authorities, equipping government emergency structures to deliver directly where partners are absent, and preparedness capacity building have all produced structures that later led coordination with little support — in one province, several years after the emergencies that established it. Counterparts who had previously attended cluster training made transition discussions substantially easier. Engaging before funding forces the question was identified as the working model rather than the exception.

Dedicated coordination capacity placed where delivery happens improves alignment. Subnational coordination leadership strengthens engagement with local authorities and enables bottom-up planning; operational hubs with dedicated subnational staffing and district-level area groups anchored a major drought scale-up; and full subnational coverage gives a sector enough technical standing to question fragmented parallel structures when they are proposed.

Where a dedicated sector information management post ended, capacity has been rebuilt as a shared resource rather than replaced one-for-one: a pool serving all agency-led sectors in a field office, comparable pools at sub-district level drawing staff from UN agencies, NGOs and government rather than a single agency, and short deployments used to build the capacity of volunteer information officers covering more than one sector.

Lightweight tools built on common office software have reduced the information management workload: a database returning results by indicator from data pasted out of the reporting platform, and a web application routing partner requests for prepositioned supplies through the cluster to a government approver, replacing a paper process that made donor reporting difficult.

Structured peer exchange is asked for repeatedly and works where it is run. Government counterparts want to learn directly from countries where coordination has already moved to government, rather than from guidance material alone. Regular discussion meetings among subnational focal points, and rolling training for state coordinators developed alongside the tools it teaches, were both well received and asked to continue.

Handover needs an accompaniment period rather than a cut-over. Continued technical support acts as a safety net for newly established successor mechanisms, and the arrangements documented as working are specific: a six-month post-handover mentoring phase with quarterly reviews, twelve-month transition advisers covering all sectors, external surge teams managing complex handovers to government, and direct mentoring of national co-facilitators.

Build the successor's capacity deliberately and anchor it institutionally rather than in individuals. Assess capacity at national and subnational level before handover. Set out what the support covers — coordination mechanics, emergency preparedness and response planning, contingency planning, aligned monitoring tools, logistics and supply, finance and human resources, community approaches and fundraising — rather than assuming an incoming organisation can absorb the role. Use realistic staffing models that reduce reliance on double-hatting and temporary arrangements.

Protect information management and coordination capacity through the transition. Coordinator and IM posts are consistently the first reduction in a budget cut, and deactivation has been used as a budget instrument. Treat information management as core coordination infrastructure: harmonise data systems, improve interoperability, agree common technical validation and enable joint analysis, so that what is handed over is a working system rather than a set of files.

Plan re-activation before deactivation. Embed coordination checkpoints in emergency preparedness plans and digital preparedness platforms so that preparedness reviews ask who convenes and who does information management in the next emergency. Run annual refreshers with transitioned countries, keep contact lists and awareness of surge options current, and agree in writing who calls for help. A flash appeal should not suspend a transition plan: commit at senior level that the actors being capacitated stay in the room, because the emergency is the best available learning environment for a successor structure. Sectoral readiness accountability remains with the cluster lead agency as well as with government after deactivation. A support package exists — a transition chapter in the coordination toolkit, training for coordination teams, customisable in-country training for successor authorities, a helpdesk and standby deployments.
